page.title: Journal and replay
page.description: Record every input your program gives a tinyactors host, and replay the journal to rebuild every actor after a crash, without running any effect again.

hero.headline: Rebuild a host from its inputs
hero.lede: A chart's state follows from its inputs and their times. Write each input to a journal before the host sees it, and one loop rebuilds every actor without charging a card again.

section.heading: Your program already has a log
section.p: A crash stops every actor in the process. What comes back is what your program wrote down (what a crash keeps).
tinyactors writes no log of its own, because your program already has one: a table, a file, a queue. Recording an input is one write, and replaying is one loop.
A chart that reads no clock and no random numbers has no hidden inputs. Given the same events in the same order at the same times, it takes the same transitions and ends in the same state.

section.heading: Record every input, then apply it
section.p: An order takes two items and checks out. The payment service never answers the first charge, so the chart charges again 30 seconds later, and the provider's webhook then says paid.
Every input goes through one function, record(), which writes the host's time and the input, then applies it. The replay applies the same lines to a new host:
Five inputs rebuilt the order. The live host charged twice, because the chart retried after its timeout; the replay charged nothing. What each part does:

item.text: writes host.now() and the input as one JSON line, and only then applies it, so the journal never misses an input the host saw. In production, make the write durable before applying (an fsync, a committed transaction). A crash between the write and the apply replays an input the host never saw. A sender that never heard back may send it again, so give such inputs a sendid the chart checks.
the journal reaches the order by its address, tinyactors://shop/@order-1, so it reads the same on any host.
is an input like any other. An answer from outside the host must be recorded, or the replay never hears it.
does nothing, so no card is charged again. Effects leave the chart as events, which is what lets the replay switch them off.
moves to each entry's time and runs everything due by then before applying the entry, so the 30-second timeout fires before the webhook arrives, as it did live.
takes a snapshot of the replayed host and runs it on the runtime's clock with the real processor, so the program goes on where it stopped.

section.heading: Keep the journal short with snapshots
section.p: A journal that is never cut grows with every input, and so does the replay. Snapshot the host now and then, and store the journal's position with the snapshot.
After a crash, restore the last snapshot on a SimulatedClock and replay only the entries after it. Then snapshot again and empty the journal (replay the inputs that came after).
The turn-game example does this for a game server it kills and restarts. It checkpoints every second and replays the moves made since.

section.heading: Keep the chart's inputs in the journal
section.p: A replay matches only when every input the chart reads is in the journal. Check three things.

item.text: a chart that reads Date or Math.random gets a new answer on replay. Read them in your program and pass them in as event data, which the journal then holds.

an I/O processor's answer, a service's sendBack and done and a host.fail are inputs. Give them through record(), with the sender's address and the send's sendid, and on replay give the processors and services stand-ins that do nothing.

the replay runs every timer due at an entry's time before the entry, while live the input may have come first. A chart should not depend on which wins within one millisecond, as a move against its turn's timeout in the turn-game example does.

a charge the live host sent, whose answer never reached the journal, is lost with the crash. After the restore, the chart's timer charges again, so send the same idempotency key on every attempt (one key for every attempt).

section.heading: Journal a host, or one actor
section.p: When actors send each other events, one actor's input changes another's state. Journal the whole host, the unit a replay rebuilds.
An actor that hears only from outside can have a journal of its own, keyed by its name. Replay that journal into a fresh host to rebuild it alone.

section.heading: Choose a journal, snapshots or both

item.text: keeps every input, so nothing after the last write is lost, and it doubles as an audit log. It costs one write before each input and a replay as long as the journal.
cost nothing per input, and restoring two million actors took 0.14 to 0.21 s (measured on one machine). Inputs after the last snapshot are lost.
restore the last snapshot, then replay the short journal written since. This is what turn-game does.
is not a log: it keeps waiting actors out of memory. Use it with either.
